paper_title: InfiniDream: Open-Ended Photorealistic 3D Worlds Through Procedural Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Procedural generation plays a key role in synthetic data creation and game development, offering greater controllability, editability, and diversity than static mesh representations. However, VLM-based code generation often produces relatively simple 3D assets, while sophisticated photorealistic procedural systems require extensive manual development. Existing VLM-guided procedural methods remain largely constrained by predefined factories and APIs, limiting their ability to create novel asset types. We introduce InfiniDream, a VLM-driven framework for open-ended procedural 3D world generation. First, we propose Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation, which leverages existing procedural algorithms to create novel, photorealistic assets while preserving editability and seed-based diversity. Second, we develop an end-to-end text-to-world pipeline that combines semantic scene planning with Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement to construct large-scale 3D worlds with precise object placement, procedural population, and animation. Extensive evaluations on 100 object and 20 scene generation tasks demonstrate improvements across four perceptual metrics. Diversity analysis, ablation studies, and human preference evaluations further validate the effectiveness of our framework. Project page: https://yichuanh.github.io/infinidream-page/

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Procedural generation creates 3D assets and scenes through executable programs, offering editability, diversity, and scalability. These advantages have made it widely applicable to synthetic data generation, 1 Figure 2 Motivation: Beyond predefined procedural factories. Given flowering cactus desert prompt, VLM-based code generation produces simplified geometry, predefined factories offer limited variations, and parameter-based generation struggles to introduce new features. InfiniDream extends existing procedural generators to create novel assets within rich, photorealistic 3D worlds. game development, and virtual world creation [70]. However, conventional procedural generation methods rely heavily on handcrafted rules and predefined asset generators, limiting the variety of generated content and their ability to create novel assets and scenes. Recent advances in the code generation and tool-use capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) have enabled the generation and editing of 3D assets and scenes through executable Blender code [28, 55, 73, 110, 24, 96]. However, while existing approaches can construct scenes by composing assets or directly synthesizing geometry through code, generating large-scale 3D scenes with consistently rich geometric details, complex materials, and photorealistic appearance remains challenging. Infinigen [70] is built on over 40,000 lines of code, including carefully handcrafted procedural asset factories, to generate photorealistic, editable 3D scenes. However, its generative capabilities remain constrained by predefined asset categories and procedural rules. Recent studies have explored using LLMs and VLMs to control sophisticated procedural generation systems through function orchestration, parameter adjustment, and the composition of existing generators [82, 119, 117]. While these approaches improve the controllability of procedural scene generation, methods that primarily operate within predefined functions and parameter spaces remain limited in their ability to create novel asset types beyond the capabilities of existing generators. Another line of research explores large-scale 3D world generation using retrieved or generatively synthesized mesh assets [23, 92]. Although these methods support instance-level editing, their mesh-based assets lack the parameterized editability and seed-based diversity of procedural generators. Producing diverse object variations often requires direct mesh manipulation or regeneration. Figure 2 highlights three limitations: VLM Harness produces less photorealistic scenes, Infinigen is restricted to predefined factories, and Code2Worlds [117], recent VLM-guided Infinigen framework, is limited to function calls and parameter adjustment. These limitations motivate open-ended procedural generation beyond existing factory capabilities. To address these challenges, we introduce InfiniDream, VLM-driven framework for open-ended procedural 3D world generation, designed to achieve realism, openendedness, editability, diversity, and scalability. By employing VLM reasoning to compose and extend sophisticated procedural programs, InfiniDream generates novel assets beyond predefined factories while leveraging existing procedural algorithms. Our framework enables the creation of photorealistic, editable, and diverse large-scale 3D worlds from natural language descriptions. At the asset level, Fig. 3 further motivates our Symbolically Constrained Editing (SCE) strategy, which combines the flexibility of VLM-based code generation with the rich procedural structures of existing factories. Figure 3 Comparison of procedural asset generation strategies. From left to right: VLM-generated Blender code from scratch, predefined Infinigen factories, VLM Agent Harness with full Infinigen access, and our symbolically constrained editing. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: 1. Open-Ended Procedural Asset Generation. We propose Symbolically Constrained Editing (SCE) to generate novel, photorealistic procedural assets with rich geometric details beyond predefined factories, while preserving editability and seed-based diversity. 2. Scalable Procedural World Generation. We introduce an end-to-end text-to-world framework combining semantic scene planning and deterministic frustum-guided grid placement to generate large-scale, editable 3D worlds. 3. Comprehensive Experimental Validation. We conduct extensive objectand scene-level evaluations, diversity analysis, ablation studies, and human preference studies to validate the effectiveness of InfiniDream.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Procedural 3D Asset Generation. Procedural modeling encodes 3D content as executable rules, from Lsystems [50, 66] and shape grammars [97, 60] to learned procedural shape and CAD programs [77, 89, 36, 37, 38, 72, 98, 41]. Advances in code generation [4] and tool use [75, 109] now let language models synthesize editable 3D assets as Blender code [13, 55, 73, 96, 105, 9, 69], other shape programs [114, 39, 94, 49], or CAD scripts for mechanical parts [2, 93, 74, 57]. Multimodal reasoning, retrieval augmentation [43], and iterative visual feedback [2, 93, 94, 49] further improve reconstruction, editing, and visual fidelity [29, 110, 24, 96]. Procedural material graphs are likewise generated or inferred from images [78, 21, 27, 44, 45], whereas inverse procedural modeling fits predefined procedural generators to targets [85, 91, 81, 63, 118] and remains bounded by their categories. Still, reliably synthesizing complex procedural geometry with rich geometric details and photorealistic appearance remains challenging. Benchmarks for 3D code generation [19, 96, 13, 2, 20, 107, 52] assess executability, geometric fidelity, and the benefits of execution feedback [6] and agentic coding [106]. However, 3DCodeBench [19] draws its procedural modeling categories from predefined Infinigen factories [70, 71], leaving procedural asset generation beyond these categories underexplored. 3D World Generation. Procedural content generation [80, 25, 76] has long produced noise-based terrains [64, 61] and cities [62], and now yields photorealistic natural and indoor scenes [70, 71, 69], simulation-ready assets [40], and houses for embodied AI [11]. Language models have been leveraged for 3D scene planning, spatial reasoning, and executable scene construction [28, 82, 119, 117, 15, 108, 3, 17, 83, 1, 116, 86, 22], and one line couples them with existing procedural generators through function orchestration, parameter adjustment, and composition of predefined procedural assets [82, 119, 67, 117, 115, 53, 87, 54]. Related approaches [28, 110, 117] also explore hierarchical generation [17, 84, 95], iterative visual feedback [51], physics-aware dynamic simulation [56], and looping animation of static 3D scenes [103]. However, methods restricted to orchestrating predefined procedural generators remain confined to their asset categories and parameter spaces, while semantically consistent and geometrically precise object placement in complex scenes remains challenging. Another line of work builds large-scale worlds [23, 92] from procedural layouts, retrieved assets [10, 108, 1, 12], generative 3D models [65, 26, 113, 101], and object-level composition [95, 31, 59], expanding generatable content and enabling instance-level manipulation. However, these approaches and neural scene generators [35, 46, 16, 112, 111, 88, 30, 5, 8, 18, 120, 14, 7, 48, 102, 42, 99, 58] generally lack the reusable procedural structures and high-level parameters needed for procedural editing and seed-based geometric variation. Orthogonally, recent work decouples explicit world states from generative video rendering [32, 34, 47] and benchmarks whether video models render what program specifies [33]; such systems still require an explicit world specification, which procedural world generation can supply. InfiniDream addresses these gaps: it enables open-ended procedural asset generation beyond predefined factories and integrates it into scalable, fully procedural 3D world generation, while preserving procedural editability and seed-based diversity. 3 Figure 4 Procedural asset generation through SCE. (A) Factory mapping and retrieval. (B) Structured editing plan. (C) Coarse asset construction. (D) Render-guided fine refinement. Existing procedural algorithms are reused under explicit editing constraints.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: We introduce InfiniDream, VLM-driven framework for open-ended procedural 3D world generation. Given text prompt, our framework selects suitable initial scene and employs Director to produce structured Scene Plan specifying asset requirements, semantic placement constraints, and motion. Our framework consists of two core components: Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation, which creates novel procedural assets through constrained editing, and Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement, which translates semantic constraints into precise 3D object placements. Finally, procedural asset pooling, terrain refinement, and animation enable diverse, large-scale world generation.

sections.title: 3.1 Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation
sections.content: Since directly providing VLM with the entire Infinigen codebase often leads to imprecise editing  (Fig. 3)  , we propose Symbolically Constrained Editing (SCE), which extracts key code structures and explicit editing constraints, transforming large procedural codebase into manageable editing space  (Fig. 4)  . 3.1.1 Factory Mapping and Retrieval Given text description and an optional reference image, the system retrieves the most relevant Infinigen factory and constructs Factory Brief (Fig. 4(A)). It contains Code Structure Map identifying key functions and dependencies, an Editable Surface consisting of asset-specific modules dynamically identified through depth-limited dependency analysis, and Linked Infrastructure providing read-only access to shared lowlevel algorithms (e.g., node graphs) via symbolic links. Together, these components establish explicit code-level constraints that restrict editing while preserving the underlying procedural algorithms. Further implementation details are provided in Appendix G. 3.1.2 Structured Planning and Coarse Construction The Planner produces structured Editing Plan specifying the editing strategy (Strategy), target locations (Locate), required modifications (Edit), dependencies (Rely-on), and potential risks (Risks), as shown in Fig. 4(B). The plan also accounts for seed-dependent logic to preserve controllable procedural variation. We define three editing strategies: Tweak adjusts existing parameters and high-level logic; Create introduces new procedural functions; and Promote selectively extends editing permissions to protected modules when necessary. These strategies enable controlled expansion of the editing space. The Coarse Constructor executes the Editing Plan under these constraints (Fig. 4(C)), preserving the original factory entry points and function signatures to maintain compatibility with the population pipeline and random seed control. It reuses existing algorithms to construct coarse procedural asset. SCE preserves seed-dependent randomness by adjusting sampling ranges rather than fixing parameters to match the reference image. 4 Figure 5 Overview of InfiniDreams end-to-end world generation pipeline. (A) Scene Picker collects the user instruction and current scene information. (B) Director generates structured Scene Plan. (C) Asset Generator creates procedural assets. (D) Deterministic frustum-guided placement identifies valid object locations. (E) Population instantiates diverse assets. (F) Terrain refinement and rendering produce the final scene. 3.1.3 Fine Refinement As shown in Fig. 4(D), the Reviser iteratively compares rendered results with the target description and reference image, identifying discrepancies in geometry, materials, and visual details. It then performs targeted code modifications within the established editing boundaries. Selector identifies the best candidate across refinement iterations. Through constrained editing and iterative refinement, SCE generates novel procedural assets while preserving procedural editability and seed-controlled diversity.

sections.title: 3.2 Semantic Placement Reasoning
sections.content: Given text prompt and current scene information, the Director first formulates natural-language plan and converts it into structured Scene Plan specifying editing operations (add, replace, and delete), asset requirements, and semantic placement constraints (Fig. 5(AB)). The Director selects among three placement modes: Hero for semantically significant objects, Scattering for large-area distributions, and Swarm for collective entities. Hero placement supports seven Anchoring types (rooted, upright, tilted, conform, afloat, airborne, and submerged). Semantic Target and Surface Policy further specify target regions, permissible surface types, slope limits, and support conditions. Scattering and Swarm are controlled by density, coverage, and group size. The Director also determines the instance count N, distinct procedural prototypes K, World Motion, and Local Animation. World Motion specifies object trajectories and swept envelopes for collision checking. VLM decisions are restricted to discrete semantic operations and constraints, leaving continuous geometric computations to deterministic placement.

sections.title: 3.3 Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement
sections.content: To avoid repeated VLM-based coordinate prediction and costly render-based verification, we propose Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement, which translates the Directors semantic constraints into 5 candidate 3D positions (Fig. 5(D)). Candidates are evaluated in near-to-far order without additional VLM calls or iterative rendering. 3.3.1 Frustum-based Candidate Generation Given the specified placement region, we discretize the cameras image plane into 2D grid and generate 3D candidate positions along the corresponding camera rays. For surface-supported objects, candidates are determined by ray intersections with scene geometry. For airborne and submerged objects, candidates are sampled at discrete depth intervals along each ray. 3.3.2 Constraint-based Filtering and Depth-aware Placement Each candidate undergoes five deterministic checks: (1) Visibility, (2) Collision with motion swept envelopes, (3) Inter-instance Spacing, (4) Surface Policy, including surface type, slope limits, and full support, and (5) Projected-area Band, requiring amin a(p) amax. sections.content: We combine the procedural assets generated in Sec. 3.1 with the validated placements from Sec. 3.3 through semantically controlled asset pooling, terrain refinement, and procedural animation (Fig. 5(E)). Semantically Budgeted Asset Pooling. To reduce the repeated construction cost of complex procedural assets, we extend Infinigens asset pooling mechanism to independent object population. Population, Terrain Refinement, and Animation. Procedural assets are placed according to their Anchoring modes and integrated with Infinigens fine terrain pipeline. Animation combines World Motion and Local Animation, with shared motion specifications ensuring consistency between placement constraints and actual trajectories. The final scene is then refined and rendered (Fig. 5(EF)).

sections.title: 4.1 Evaluation Protocol and Baselines
sections.content: Object-level Evaluation. We compare InfiniDream against five baselines: VLM (one-shot), VLM (harness), VIGA [110], BlenderRAG [73], and Infinigen [70]. Following 3DCodeBench [19], we adopt its codebase for the two VLM baselines, evaluating single-turn code generation and iterative refinement with native coding-agent harness. The remaining baselines represent visual-feedback refinement, retrieval-augmented generation, and original Infinigen factory outputs, respectively. Scene-level Evaluation. We compare large-scale world generation against VLM (harness), VIGA [110], Infinigen [70], and Code2Worlds [117], representing agentic code generation, visual-feedback refinement, original procedural scene generation, and LLM-driven hierarchical procedural orchestration, respectively. Implementation and Metrics. We use Claude Opus 4.8 for InfiniDream and all VLM-based baselines, with Blender 4.x for generation and rendering. We evaluate 100 object-level tasks across six categories and 20 scene-level tasks at resolutions of 1024 1024 and 960 540, respectively. We report CLIP [68], SigLIP2 [90], DINOv3 [79], and ImageReward [104]. At the object level, CLIP, SigLIP2, and ImageReward are averaged over four fixed views (45, 135, 225, and 315), while DINOv3 compares the front view against four held-out reference images, independently generated from the same text prompt, and reports the mean cosine similarity. We additionally report code executability. Scene-level metrics use each methods primary camera view. For scene-level DINOv3, each methods primary camera view is compared against single per-prompt scene reference image, generated by Gemini 3 Pro Image from the same scene prompt as photorealistic wide-angle photograph of the entire scene; the same reference is shared by all methods and is never provided to any method during generation. Further details are provided in the Appendix. Diversity Evaluation. We compare InfiniDream with TRELLIS.2 [100] on 15 text prompts. For each prompt, InfiniDream generates five variations using different random seeds, while TRELLIS.2 uses five independently generated reference images. We measure semantic consistency using SigLIP2 and visual diversity using average pairwise DINOv2 feature distance.

sections.title: 4.4 Ablation Studies
sections.content: Object-level Ablation Figure 10 Qualitative scene-level placement ablation. Visual comparison of different placement strategies, illustrating the effects of semantic planning, grid-based placement, and anchoring constraints on object visibility, spatial arrangement, and scene composition. We evaluate six ablation settings on 25 animal and plant tasks: (1) w/o Ref. Image, (2) Random Factory, (3) w/o Planner, (4) Agent (Infinigen), (5) w/o Refiner, and (6) 3 Rounds. The full pipeline allows up to six refinement rounds. For Agent (Infinigen), Claude Opus 4.8 is given the entire Infinigen codebase and Bash access to autonomously write and edit code, render and inspect results, and determine when to stop within six rounds, without our structured planning or editing constraints. Quantitative and qualitative results are shown in Table 5 and Fig. 9. Scene-level Ablation. We evaluate four settings on 20 scenes: (1) w/o Grid Search, using direct 3D coordinate prediction; (2) w/o Anchoring, reverting to Infinigens grounding; (3) w/o Semantic Target, removing semantic surface constraints; and (4) Agent (Placement), allowing VLM agent to autonomously place our generated 3D assets in the same selected coarse scene given the text prompt, without our placement pipeline. We evaluate three placement metrics: Unreadable Rate, the percentage of objects outside the camera view or occupying less than 0.1% of the image area; Ground-contact Error, the absolute distance between an objects lowest contact point and its supporting surface, capturing floating or penetration; and Contact Spread, the difference between the maximum and minimum terrain-relative gaps across sampled contact points, capturing uneven grounding and partial suspension (surface-supported objects only; see Appendix J). We report the 95th percentile (P95) for the latter two metrics. For Contact Spread, P95 is computed over per-object values pooled across all surface-supported requested-add objects in the 20 scenes. Results are shown in Table 6 and Fig. 10.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented InfiniDream, VLM-driven framework for open-ended procedural 3D world generation. By combining Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation with semantic planning and deterministic placement, 9 InfiniDream creates novel, photorealistic, and editable procedural assets and composes them into diverse, large-scale 3D worlds. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness at both the object and scene levels. Limitations and Future Work. Our current animation pipeline relies on predefined set of motion types. Future work could explore VLM-generated animation code to support more complex and customized motions. We also aim to extend InfiniDream to indoor environments with more complex spatial relationships and object interactions.

sections.title: G Implementation Details of Symbolically Constrained Editing
sections.content: Reference Synthesis and Factory Retrieval. We use Gemini 3 Pro Image to generate an isolated reference object against white background. Claude Opus 4.8 retrieves the most relevant Infinigen factory, with deterministic lexical matching as fallback. Factory Brief Construction. Starting from the selected factory, we perform AST-based import graph traversal with maximum depth of two. Asset-specific modules form the Editable Surface, while shared modules remain read-only Linked Infrastructure. Unrelated dependencies are pruned, and VLM summarizes the remaining code into cached Code Structure Map. Constrained Code Editing. The Planner produces an Editing Plan specifying Strategy, Locate, Edits, Rely-on, and Risks. The Constructor can modify existing modules (Tweak), promote protected modules (Promote), or synthesize new procedural modules (Create). Editing is restricted to the working directory, preserving the original factory interface and seed-dependent randomness. Iterative Refinement. Modified modules are integrated into symbolic-link overlay of the original Infinigen codebase. vision-based Reviser guides targeted refinement, while execution failures trigger tracebackbased repair. The pipeline supports up to six rounds with early stopping. vision-based Selector chooses the best successful candidate, whose code snapshot is used to reconstruct the final executable generator. Implementation Details of Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement Candidate Generation. We discretize the Directors screen-space region into 9 5 grid (17 9 for six or more instances). Surface candidates are obtained through ray-scene intersections, while airborne and submerged candidates are sampled along camera rays using geometric depth intervals (1.3, up to 80 m). Larger objects are placed first, with deterministic hashing ensuring reproducibility. The entire placement process requires no additional VLM calls. Constraints and Relaxation. Projected area is estimated from the proxy bounding box, with preferred minimum of 1.2%, relaxed minimum of 0.2%, and an absolute maximum of 25%. Collision checks account for motion-dependent swept envelopes, while surface placement additionally enforces slope limits and four-corner footprint support. When no valid candidate is found, constraints are progressively relaxed and the search region is expanded. Water-related constraints remain enforced, and all relaxations are recorded in the resulting placement plan.

sections.title: I Baseline Implementation Details
sections.content: Baseline Implementations. We adopt the official implementations of all baselines, adding Claude Opus 4.8 API adapters where necessary. The VLM (one-shot) and VLM (harness) baselines follow 3DCodeBench, with the latter supporting autonomous code execution and iterative refinement. SigLIP2 Score Computation. All SigLIP2 scores in this paper (Tables 1, 2, 4, 5, 7) are computed with google/siglip2-base-patch16-224 and reported as the cosine similarity between L2-normalized image and text embeddings, recovered from the models imagetext logits via cos = (logit b)/t, where = 112.67 and = 16.77 are SigLIP2s learned temperature and bias. Scores are averaged over the four azimuth views at the object level (Tables 1, 5, 7), the primary camera view at the scene level  (Table 2)  , and the five variations per prompt in the diversity evaluation  (Table 4)  . Object-level Baselines. All methods receive identical text prompts and reference images, except BlenderRAG, which only supports text inputs. Each task has five Gemini-generated reference images: ref_00 is the conditioning reference provided to the generation methods, while ref_01ref_04 are held out exclusively for evaluation (DINOv3) and the human study and are never shown to any method; the conditioning 22 reference is never used for scoring. All assets are evaluated under identical camera, lighting, background, and rendering settings. Failed generations are retained as blank renders rather than excluded. Scene-level Baselines. All scene-level methods receive identical text prompts and follow their respective official scene generation and camera selection pipelines. For InfiniDream, the Scene Picker automatically retrieves the most relevant initial coarse scene based on the input prompt from library of 70 pre-generated environments (14 biomes with five seeds each), which is then used as the basis for subsequent procedural editing. The library was built before the benchmark prompts were finalized and was not modified afterwards. For reproducibility, the Scene Pickers selection is made once per task, and the chosen base scene and seed are then fixed across all benchmark and ablation runs. The other baselines do not use this library. Code2Worlds selects from its available procedural factories even when no closely matching category exists. Failure Handling. We resolve versionand environment-related execution issues wherever possible to ensure that baselines run as intended. We do not report separate scene-level executability metric.

sections.title: J Ablation Study Details
sections.content: Object-level Ablation. We provide additional implementation details for the six ablation settings: (1) w/o Ref. Image removes the reference image from the generation pipeline; (2) Random Factory replaces factory retrieval with random selection; (3) w/o Planner removes structured planning and replaces the Editing Plan with empty content; (4) Agent (Infinigen) gives Claude Opus 4.8 coding-agent harness access to the entire Infinigen codebase and Bash tools, allowing autonomous code generation, rendering, and refinement without SCE constraints, for up to six rounds; (5) w/o Refiner removes fine-level refinement; and (6) 3 Rounds limits the refinement budget to three rounds, compared with six in the full method. Scene-level Ablation. We evaluate four placement variants: (1) w/o Grid Search removes discrete semantic planning and grid-based placement, allowing the Director to predict continuous 3D coordinates directly; (2) w/o Anchoring replaces our seven anchoring types with Infinigens original grounding mechanism; (3) w/o Semantic Target removes semantic surface constraints from grid search, allowing placements on semantically inappropriate surfaces; and (4) Agent (Placement) provides VLM agent with our generated 3D assets, the text prompt, and the same selected coarse scene, allowing autonomous placement without our placement pipeline. Contact Spread. For each object, we select the lowest 12% of sampled points and cluster them into four contact regions using k-means. The lowest point in each region is selected, and its vertical gap to the underlying terrain is computed via ray casting. Contact Spread is defined as the difference between the maximum and minimum gaps, capturing uneven grounding independently of terrain elevation. Both contact metrics are computed only for surface-supported objects (rooted, upright, tilted, conform, and afloat; afloat is measured against the water surface); airborne and submerged objects are excluded, while the Unreadable Rate covers all placed objects. Ground-contact Error uses the absolute gap, so floating and penetration both count by magnitude. Objects whose contact rays find no supporting surface, or that failed to populate, are excluded. P95 is the nearest-rank 95th percentile of per-object values pooled across all surface-supported requested-add objects in the 20 scenes. For Agent (Placement), anchoring types are inferred from the full-pipeline runs; objects without counterpart, and plant assets whose lowest vertices are foliage rather than ground contacts, are excluded from its contact statistics.

sections.title: L Human Evaluation Details
sections.content: Figure 17 Human evaluation interface. Participants compare anonymized generation results and independently select their preferred method for semantic alignment and visual quality at both the object and scene levels. Study Setup. We conduct forced-choice preference study on 10 object and 10 scene generation tasks. For each object, participants are shown the text prompt, held-out reference image not provided to any generation method, and front-view renders (1024 1024) from six methods: InfiniDream, BlenderRAG, VIGA, VLM (one-shot), VLM (harness), and Infinigen. For each scene, participants compare 5-second orbit videos (854 480) from five methods: InfiniDream, VIGA, VLM (harness), Code2Worlds, and Infinigen. All results are presented without cropping or background normalization. The object subset covers animals, marine life, plants, and natural props, while the scene subset spans seven 24 distinct environment types. Evaluation Protocol. As illustrated in Fig. 17, all methods are anonymized, and both task order and method positions are randomized independently for each participant. Each task contains two forced-choice questions evaluating semantic alignment and visual quality. For objects, participants select the result that best matches the description and reference image, and the result with the highest 3D quality. For scenes, participants evaluate text alignment and overall scene realism, considering object placement, naturalness, and visual artifacts. Each participant completes 40 judgments across both levels. We recruit 30 participants, yielding 20 judgments per level per participant.
